newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sanctions Chinese companies for Iran sales.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sanctions Chinese companies for Iran sales.

text.p: The United States toughened its position on China on Thursday, imposing new sanctions on Chinese companies for transferring chemical weapons components to Iran.

Testifying before Congress, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright insisted "there is no evidence the Chinese government was involved" in the transfers, which involved chemicals and other technology that could be used in chemical weapons.
However, the State Department said Washington had asked Beijing to halt the transfers but there was "no evidence" that the Chinese government had complied.

The sanctions were imposed on two Chinese companies -- Nanjing Chemical Industries Group and Jiangsu Yongli Chemical Engineering and Technology Import/Export Corp -- and a Hong Kong company, Cheong Yee Limited.
Also, five Chinese citizens were penalized: Liao Minglong, Tian Yi, Chen Qingchang, Pan Yongming and Shao Xingsheng.

"We think that Iran's chemical weapons program is the largest in the developing world (and that) Iran continues to expand its chemical weapons program despite the fact that it signed the Chemical Weapons Convention" banning the production, stockpiling and use of such weapons, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing.

The action marks the first time Chinese entities have been penalized under the Chemical and Biological Weapons Control and Warfare Elimination Act of 1991, although persons and companies in other countries have had sanctions imposed, officials said.

In her testimony to the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Foreign Operations, Albright said: "We do share your deep concern about what is going on" in the cooperation between China and Iran on weapons-related programs.

Officials said the sanctioned parties were accused of transferring glass-lined chemical processing equipment and three dual-use chemicals -- thionyl chloride, diamethylamine and ethylene chlorohydrine -- to Iran.

Officials said the sanctions prohibit the United States from procuring any goods or services from the affected individuals and entities for at least one year. Also, the sanctioned entities and persons are barred form importing any products to the United States in that period.
For the sanctions to be terminated, the president must certify to Congress that the individuals and entities have ceased to abet Iran's program, Burns said.

Burns said the United States had raised its concerns about Chinese chemical transfers on repeated occasions with Chinese officials, including with Foreign Minister Qian Qichen when he met Albright in Washignton last month.
"We hoped they (Chinese officials) would be aggressive in acting to halt the sales but I can't say I have any evidence," Burns told a news briefing.
He noted that China had several times stated publicly its commitment to the Chemical Weapons Convention and is opposed to the development of chemical weapons by any other country.

"We hope that this (sanctions) action will serve to encourage the Chinese government to improve its export controls to make them much more effective so they can prevent Chinese entities from assisting Iran in the future," he said.

The sanctions were imposed after increasing criticism from members of Congress who argue the administration has doggedly pursued improved ties with China despite concerns about Beijing's arms cooperation with Iran, its human rights record, its trade surplus and fears that rights will erode when Hong Kong reverts from British to Chinese control on July 1.

But the decision was made after Clinton announced he would renew for one year Most Favored Nation trade benefits for China, something Beijing keenly desires but which is also drawing congressional fire.

Also, the administration made the clear point of putting the onus on the Chinese entities -- not Beijing. Sanctioning the government likely would have sent Sino-American relations into another tailspin during a year in which Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin plan to hold a summit this fall.
